newsitem.title: CHINA: China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping dies.
newsitem.headline: China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping dies.

text.p: through)
By Jane Macartney
China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping died late on Wednesday after an 18-year rule in which China transformed itself from backward Stalinist state to economic powerhouse. He was 92.

A letter from the ruling Communist Party, the People's Liberation Army and China's people expressed profound grief at the death of "a great Marxist, a great proletarian revolutionary, statesman, military strategist and diplomat".
The gravel-voiced veteran of the battlefield and political struggle died at 9.08 p.m. (1308 GMT) in Beijing, the official Xinhua news agency said.
Deng, whose pragmatic economic reforms propelled China onto the world stage as a major player, was in the advanced stages of Parkinson's disease with complications from lung infections.
He died of respiratory failure after he did not respond to emergency treatment, Xinhua said.

Chinese sources close to the party said doctors performed an emergency tracheotomy in an attempt to save Deng before he died, reportedly in the crimson-walled Zhongnanhai government compound just off Tiananmen Square.
Deng was 92 but the official announcement listed his age as 93. He was born on August 22, 1904, but China adds a year to a person's age.

The party and government "proclaim with profound grief to the whole party, the whole army and the people of all ethnic groups throughout the country that our beloved Comrade Deng Xiaoping... passed away", Xinhua said.

Deng died without achieving one of his dreams -- to be present in Hong Kong when the colony, wrested from China at gunpoint by the British as spoils of victory in the opium wars, returns to the mainland rule at midnight on June 30 this year.

China said no foreign dignitaries would be invited to the funeral and flags would fly at half-mast in Tiananmen Square and at the Great Hall of the People, as well at Chinese embassies around the world "to express the incomparable esteem and profound grief of the whole Party, the whole army and the people".
Condolences began pouring in for Deng, who had not been seen in public since the Chinese lunar new year festival in 1994 when he appeared frail and faltering on a visit to Shanghai.
U.S. President Bill Clinton said he was saddened to learn of Deng's death, calling him an "extraordinary figure on the world stage over the past two decades".
Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien expressed regret over Deng's death but said his feelings were mixed because of Deng's record on human rights.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was saddened by Deng's death and pledged to "continue to work with China's leaders for the long-term stability of our bilateral relationship".

Deng died almost within sight of Tiananmen Square, where troops and tanks of the People's Liberation Army, acting on Deng's orders, crushed student-led demonstrations for more democracy with heavy loss of life in 1989.

Analysts said chances were faint for an immediate factional struggle in the upper echelons of China's internecine political world, because Deng's anointed heir, Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin had a firm grip on power.
Factory manager and technocrat Jiang has already amassed the positions of Communist Party chief, state President and head of the armed forces.

Streets were quiet and calm after China's the early morning announcement, but additional police patrolled outside the Zhongnanhai compound and military cars with flashing lights drove along main city streets.
Two armed police carrying assault rifles stood guard at the end of the lane in central Beijing where Deng had lived.
Visitors in small groups were going in and out of the compound where Deng lived, on a leafy alley behind the Forbidden City that once housed China's emperors.
Xinhua issued a lengthy obituary filled with praise for the man who came to power in 1978 after being purged three times and who retired only in 1990. His influence reigned supreme until his death.
"Comrade Deng Xiaoping was an outstanding leader enjoying high prestige acknowledged by the Party, the army and the people of all ethnic groups throughout China," Xinhua said.

It called him "a long-tested communist fighter, the chief architect of China's socialist reforms, opening up and modernisation drive, and the founder of the theory of building socialism with Chinese characteristics".

The long stream of titles that did not omit any of the adjectives that China's Communist Party associates with a senior leader in a eulogy, was an official mark that the party planned to ensure Deng was buried with full party honours.
Official media gave no date for a funeral.
